nameStory: The 'marsh' part of this plant's name comes from its love of wet, boggy places where most plants would drown. 'Willowherb' refers to its narrow, willow-like leaves and its membership in a group of plants that were once thought to be related to herbs used medicinally. The scientific name 'palustre' is Latin for 'of the marsh,' doubly emphasizing this plant's preference for soggy ground.
description: Marsh willowherb is a delicate, slender wildflower that stands about 1-2 feet tall in wet meadows and boggy areas. It produces small, pale pink or white flowers with four rounded petals that bloom along the upper stem. The plant has narrow, lance-shaped leaves that grow opposite each other on smooth, often reddish stems. It's a quiet beauty that blends into marshy landscapes but rewards close observation with its intricate flower structure.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pale pink or white flowers with four rounded petals and a deeply notched appearance, about 1/4 inch across, growing in loose clusters at stem tips

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs, with smooth edges and a slightly waxy feel when rubbed between fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright stems reaching 1-2 feet tall, often growing in small colonies connected by underground runners

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, thin seed pods that split open to release fluffy white seeds that drift on the wind like tiny parachutes

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, hairless stems that are often tinged with red or purple, especially toward the base, and feel firm but not woody

habitat: Look for marsh willowherb in wet meadows, boggy areas, and the edges of ponds and streams throughout New England's mountains and northern regions. It thrives in acidic, peaty soils that stay consistently moist and prefers areas with partial shade to full sun. You'll often find it growing alongside sedges, sphagnum moss, and other moisture-loving plants.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground runners as rosettes of narrow leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from July through August with delicate pink or white flowers that open in the morning and close by afternoon on hot days.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and split open, releasing clouds of fluffy white seeds. Leaves may turn reddish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground parts, leaving no above-ground trace until spring.

funFact: Marsh willowherb has one of the widest distributions of any plant on Earth, growing in wetlands from Alaska to Labrador, down through New England's mountains, and across northern Europe and Asia - it literally circles the globe in cold, wet places!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other willowherbs, especially fringed willowherb, but marsh willowherb's preference for consistently wet ground and its smaller, paler flowers help distinguish it. Remember: if your feet are getting soggy, you might be looking at marsh willowherb rather than its drier-ground cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'herb,' willowherbs aren't closely related to culinary herbs like basil or oregano - they're actually in the evening primrose family. The 'herb' designation comes from old European traditions of using various willowherbs for folk medicine.
compareHints: Marsh willowherb is much smaller and more delicate than Great Willowherb, which can tower over 6 feet tall with showy magenta flowers. Unlike cinnamon willowherb with its tiny flowers and toothed leaves, marsh willowherb has smooth-edged leaves and noticeably larger blooms. It's also the only willowherb in New England that specifically requires constantly wet, marshy conditions to thrive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's willowherbs, cinnamon willowherb is distinguished by its colorful stems and leaves - most other willowherbs stay green throughout the season.
Among New England's willowherbs, great willowherb lives up to its name by being the tallest and most robust.
Among New England's willowherbs, fringed willowherb is distinguished by those characteristic tiny hairs along its leaf edges - no other local willowherb has this feature.
Unlike its lowland cousins like great willowherb or cinnamon willowherb, Hornemann's willowherb is much smaller in all respects - shorter stems, tinier flowers, and narrower leaves.
Among New England's willowherbs, linear-leaf willowherb has the narrowest leaves and prefers the wettest habitats.
Among New England's willowherbs, downy willowherb is distinguished by its thoroughly fuzzy texture - much more so than cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb.

Among New England willowherbs, hoary willowherb stands out for its overall grayish, densely fuzzy appearance - most other willowherbs like cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb are greener with less conspicuous hairs.
